name: Teufelberger PulleySaver
title: Teufelberger PulleySaver Friction Saver for Tree Climbing
meta: The Teufelberger PulleySaver is a friction saver with a built-in pulley for smoother doubled-rope climbing. How it works, where it fits, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A pulley-equipped friction saver for climbers who want an easier advance on doubled rope.
summary: The Teufelberger PulleySaver is a friction saver that adds a pulley at the tie-in point, so the rope runs over a sheave instead of bare metal. It protects the bark and the rope at the crotch and takes some of the work out of advancing a doubled-rope system.
highlights: Pulley at the crotch cuts friction on the advance
Protects cambium and rope at the tie-in point
Retrievable from the ground like other friction savers
Made by a long-standing rope and arborist gear maker
specs: From the ground with the climbing line

body.h: Why put a pulley in the crotch
p: A standard ring or webbing friction saver keeps your rope off the bark, but the line still bends over a fixed ring. On a long doubled-rope ascent that adds up. The PulleySaver swaps that contact point for a sheave, so the climbing line rolls rather than drags. Climbers notice it most when footlocking or body-thrusting up a tall stem, and again when they tend slack through the work position.

It also helps the tree. A friction saver keeps the rope from sawing into the bark at the tie-in point, which matters on high-value trees and on repeat pruning cycles. Browse the rest of our friction savers to compare ring, webbing, and adjustable designs.

Install and retrieve it the way the manufacturer describes, and practice the retrieval on the ground before you rely on it aloft. Make sure the crotch you choose is sound and sized for the load, and that the device sits clean without the hardware levering against the stem.

This is life-support gear. Inspect the pulley, side plates, connecting rope or webbing, and any stitching or splices before each climb. Retire it after a shock load or at the first sign of cuts, glazing, cracks, or a sheave that binds. Use it within ANSI Z133 practice and the maker's instructions, and get trained on doubled-rope climbing before you depend on any friction saver.

faq.q: Can I use the Teufelberger PulleySaver for single-rope (SRT) climbing?
faq.a: Friction savers like this are designed around doubled-rope climbing, where the rope moves through the crotch. Follow Teufelberger's instructions for the systems it is approved for.

faq.q: Is a pulley friction saver worth it over a ring saver?
faq.a: If you climb doubled rope often and want less drag on the advance, a pulley helps. A ring saver is lighter, simpler, and cheaper.

name: Yale R.I.N.G. Friction Saver
title: Yale R.I.N.G. Friction Saver for Doubled-Rope Climbing
meta: The Yale ring friction saver keeps your climbing line off the bark at the tie-in. How a ring friction saver works, how to retrieve it, and what to inspect.
tagline: A ring-style friction saver from Yale for clean, retrievable doubled-rope tie-ins.
summary: The Yale R.I.N.G. friction saver is a ring-style cambium saver: a length of rope with a ring at each end that sits in the tie-in crotch so your climbing line runs through metal instead of over bark. It is a simple, retrievable setup for doubled-rope climbers.
highlights: Keeps the climbing line off the bark
Cuts rope wear at the tie-in point
Simple ring design with no moving parts
From a well-known US arborist rope maker

body.h: How a ring friction saver works
p: Throw a line over the crotch, pull the friction saver up with the small ring leading, and run your climbing line through both rings. The line then bears on the rings instead of the bark, so the tree keeps its cambium and your rope keeps its cover. When the climb is done, a pull on the correct leg brings the small ring back through the large one and the whole thing comes down.

That retrieval step is the part to practice. Rig it wrong and the saver stays in the tree. Set one up at shoulder height and run through it until it is second nature. For other styles, including adjustable and pulley savers, see our friction savers.

A friction saver is part of your life-support system. Before each climb, check the rope body for cuts, glazing, and stiff spots, look at the splices or sewn terminations, and check the rings for grooves or burrs. Retire it if it has been shock loaded or shows damage.

Pick a tie-in that is sound and big enough for the load, and keep the rings from levering against the stem. Use it within ANSI Z133 practice and Yale's instructions, and get trained on doubled-rope climbing before relying on it.

faq.q: Why use a friction saver at all?
faq.a: It protects the bark at the tie-in, reduces wear on your climbing rope, and usually makes the advance smoother than running rope over bare wood.

faq.q: How do I get a ring friction saver back down?
faq.a: Pull the leg that draws the small ring back through the large ring, as described in the maker's instructions. Practice it on the ground first.

name: Weaver Back Pack Gear Storage Bag
keyword: weaver back pack gear storage bag
title: Weaver Back Pack Gear Storage Bag for Arborist Kit
h1: Weaver Back Pack Gear Storage Bag
meta: The Weaver back pack gear storage bag carries your saddle, hardware, and short rope on your back. What fits, how crews use it, and how to keep gear in shape.
tagline: A carry-on-your-back gear bag for climbers who walk their kit to the tree.
summary: The Weaver back pack gear storage bag lets you carry your climbing kit on your shoulders instead of in your hands. It suits climbers who park far from the tree, work in backyards past gates and fences, or just want their saddle and hardware in one place.
highlights: Room for saddle, hardware, and small rope
Keeps kit off the truck bed and out of the dirt
Easy to spot in a crowded truck
specs: Saddle, hardware, and small rope transport

p: A lot of residential work starts with a long walk: down a driveway, through a side gate, past the pool, to the back corner of the lot. Carrying a saddle in one hand and a rope bag in the other makes that walk slow and you still need a third hand for the saw. A backpack-style gear bag puts the soft kit on your back so your hands are free for the saw, the throw line, or the gate latch.

It also keeps the kit together. Saddle, lanyard, friction hitch, carabiners, and a short rope live in one bag, so the morning check is quick and nothing ends up loose in the truck. Compare sizes and styles in our gear bags.

Pack heavy hardware low and close to your back, and keep sharp items such as spurs or hand saws in their own covers so they cannot cut rope or webbing. Store the bag out of direct sun and away from fuel, bar oil, and battery acid, all of which damage textiles.

A bag is only storage. Your gear still needs its own inspection before every climb, and anything that has been crushed, soaked in chemicals, or cut needs a closer look before it goes back into service.

faq.q: Will a full saddle fit in the Weaver back pack gear bag?
faq.a: It is meant for climbing kit, including a saddle and hardware. Very large saddles with lots of attachments may be a tight fit alongside rope.

faq.q: Can I store wet gear in it?
faq.a: Dry rope and textiles before long-term storage. A closed bag holds moisture, which is hard on soft goods over time.

name: Weaver Chasm Gear Bag
title: Weaver Chasm Gear Bag for Climbing and Rigging Kit
meta: The Weaver Chasm gear bag is a roomy carry bag for climbing and rigging kit. What it holds, how tree crews use it, and tips for keeping your gear organized.
tagline: A roomy, tough gear bag for hauling climbing and rigging kit to the job.
summary: The Weaver Chasm gear bag is a large, open carry bag for the soft and hard gear a climber or rigger takes to every job. It keeps saddles, lanyards, slings, and hardware together and off the truck floor.
highlights: Holds saddle, lanyards, slings, and hardware
Easy to load and empty at the tree
Keeps kit out of the dirt and fuel

body.h: One bag for the whole kit
p: Most crews end up with gear spread across the truck: a saddle on a hook, slings in a bucket, carabiners in the door pocket. A big open gear bag like the Chasm pulls that together. At the tree, you drop it near the drop zone edge, pull what you need, and the rest stays clean and out of the way of the chipper and the brush pile.

A wide opening matters more than it sounds. You can see what is in the bag without dumping it, and coiled slings or a lanyard come out without snagging on everything else. See more sizes and styles in our gear bags.

Keep the bag away from fuel cans, bar oil, and battery terminals. Petroleum and acid are hard on rope, webbing, and stitching, and you may not see the damage until it is too late. Dry everything before it goes in for the night, and keep spurs and saws covered so they cannot cut soft goods.
The bag is not a substitute for inspection. Check each piece of life-support gear before you climb, and pull anything questionable out of service.
Many crews give each climber a bag of their own. That way every kit is checked, packed, and owned by the person who climbs on it, and nobody borrows a lanyard without knowing its history.

faq.q: Is the Weaver Chasm gear bag good for rope?
faq.a: It can carry a short rope, but a dedicated rope bag that lets the line feed out cleanly is better for climbing and rigging lines.

faq.q: How do I clean a vinyl or coated gear bag?
faq.a: Brush off dirt, wipe with mild soap and water, and let it dry open. Avoid solvents.

name: Courant Host Bag 36L
title: Courant Host Bag 36L Rope Bag for Climbers
meta: The Courant Host bag is a 36-liter rope bag that keeps your climbing line clean and ready to deploy. What it holds, how to pack it, and why a rope bag pays off.
tagline: A 36-liter Courant rope bag that keeps your line clean and ready to throw down.
summary: The Courant Host bag is a 36-liter rope bag built to carry and deploy a climbing line. Stuff the rope in, carry it to the tree, and feed it straight out of the bag without knots or a pile of dirt on the line.
highlights: 36-liter capacity for a typical climbing line
Rope feeds out cleanly from the top
Keeps grit and sap off the rope
Easy to carry from truck to tree

p: Dirt is one of the fastest ways to wear out a climbing rope. Grit works into the braid and grinds the fibers every time the rope runs through a device or over a friction saver. A rope bag like the Courant Host keeps the line off the ground at the base of the tree, out of the sawdust, and away from the chipper path.
Stuffing the rope in rather than coiling it also means it pays out cleanly. Leave the end tied to a loop in the bag so you always know where it is. For more sizes, see our rope bags.
A rope bag also speeds up the end of the day. Instead of coiling and tying off a rope in the cold or the dark, you stuff it, cinch it, and throw it in the truck, ready for the first climb tomorrow.

Thirty-six liters suits a common climbing line in the usual arborist diameters, though exact fit depends on length and construction. Longer or thicker rigging lines need a bigger bag. Pack it by feeding the rope in hand over hand from the working end, which leaves the end you need on top.
Dry the rope before long storage and keep the bag away from fuel, bar oil, and battery acid. Inspect your rope before every climb whether it lives in a bag or not.

faq.q: How much rope fits in the Courant Host bag?
faq.a: It is a 36-liter bag. How much rope fits depends on diameter and length; a typical climbing line fits, while long rigging lines need a larger bag.

faq.q: Should I coil or stuff my rope into a rope bag?
faq.a: Stuff it. Feeding it in hand over hand avoids kinks and lets it pay out cleanly.

name: Petzl 30L Rope Bucket
title: Petzl 30L Rope Bucket for Climbing Rope Storage
meta: The Petzl 30L rope bucket stands open so your climbing rope feeds in and out cleanly. How arborists use it, what size line fits, and how to care for your rope.
tagline: A 30-liter Petzl rope bucket that stays open for easy stuffing and clean deployment.
summary: The Petzl 30L rope bucket is a rope bag that holds its shape, so you can stuff a climbing line in fast and let it feed back out without tangles. It keeps the rope clean at the base of the tree and makes the walk from the truck easier.
highlights: Keeps sawdust and grit off the line

p: The difference between a rope bucket and a soft sack is speed. When the bag holds its own opening, you can feed rope in with both hands at the end of a climb without fighting the fabric. That means less time on cleanup and a rope that is ready to pay out on the next tree without snarls.
Set it near the base of the tree but out of the drop zone, and tie the tail of the rope to the bag so the end never gets lost or pulled through. Browse other sizes in our rope bags.
On a job with several climbers, separate buckets keep each person's line apart, and a quick look shows which rope is which. That small habit avoids a lot of confusion at the base of a busy tree.

Thirty liters suits a typical climbing line. Longer ropes, thicker diameters, or a second line need a bigger bag. Dry the rope before you store it for long, and keep the bucket away from fuel, bar oil, and other chemicals that can damage textiles.
Clean storage extends rope life, but it does not replace inspection. Run your hands along the line before each climb and retire it according to Petzl's guidance and ANSI Z133 practice.

faq.q: Is a 30-liter rope bucket big enough?
faq.a: For most single climbing lines, yes. Long or thick ropes, or two ropes in one bag, need more volume.

faq.q: Can I leave rope in the bucket between jobs?
faq.a: Yes, as long as it is dry and stored out of the sun and away from chemicals.

name: Reecoil Rope Bag
title: Reecoil Rope Bag for Climbing and Rigging Line
meta: The Reecoil rope bag keeps climbing and rigging line clean and ready to feed out on the job. How tree crews use a rope bag, and how to pack and store one.
tagline: A rope bag for carrying and deploying climbing or rigging line clean.
summary: The Reecoil rope bag gives your climbing or rigging line a clean home between jobs and a tidy way to deploy it at the tree. Stuff the rope in, carry it out, and let it feed out without a tangled pile.
highlights: Keeps rope out of dirt and sawdust
Easy carry from truck to tree
Keeps lines separated in the truck

p: Rope wears from the inside as much as the outside. Grit picked up off the ground works into the braid and grinds fibers every time the line runs through a device, a block, or a friction saver. A rope bag keeps the line off the ground, out of the sawdust, and away from the chipper path while you work.
Separate bags for climbing and rigging lines also help on a busy job. Nobody grabs the wrong rope, and the climbing line is not left lying under falling wood. Compare sizes in our rope bags.

Feed the rope in hand over hand from the working end and tie the tail to the bag so it cannot be lost. That leaves the end you need on top and avoids twists. Pick a bag size that matches the length and diameter of the line you plan to keep in it.
Dry rope before long storage and keep the bag away from fuel, bar oil, and battery acid. Inspect the rope itself before every climb or rigging job.
Labeling bags by rope, length, or purpose pays off on bigger crews. When someone calls for the 150-foot rigging line, the right bag comes off the truck the first time instead of after a search.

faq.q: What size rope fits in the Reecoil rope bag?
faq.a: Capacity depends on the bag size you choose. Match it to the length and diameter of your line, with a little room to spare.

faq.q: Can I use one bag for climbing and rigging rope?
faq.a: You can, but many crews keep them separate so the life-support line stays clean and easy to identify.

name: Teufelberger Kitbag
title: Teufelberger Kitbag Rope and Gear Bag for Climbers
meta: The Teufelberger Kitbag carries your climbing rope and kit in one tough bag. How tree climbers use it, packing tips, and how to keep rope and soft goods healthy.
tagline: A Teufelberger bag for carrying a climbing rope and the kit that goes with it.
summary: The Teufelberger Kitbag is a carry bag for a climbing rope and the gear that goes with it. It keeps your line and soft goods together, clean, and easy to grab when you head to the tree.
highlights: Keeps soft goods out of the dirt
Tough bag from a major arborist rope maker
Easy to carry to the work site

body.h: Rope and kit in one place
p: A climber's kit is only as good as its weakest piece, and the piece most likely to go missing is the small one: a spare hitch cord, a micro pulley, a second carabiner. Keeping rope and kit in the same bag means one grab at the truck gets you everything for the climb, and one look at the end of the day tells you it all came back.
Keeping the rope bagged at the base of the tree also keeps it out of the sawdust and away from the chipper path. See more options in our rope bags.
Stuff the rope in hand over hand so it pays out clean, and keep hardware where it will not grind against the line. Spurs and saws belong in their own covers so they cannot cut rope or webbing.

Dry the bag and its contents before storing, and keep it away from fuel, bar oil, and battery acid. A bag protects gear between jobs, but every piece still needs inspection before each climb, following the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice.

At the end of the day, empty the bag now and then and look at everything in it. Gear that rides in a bag for weeks can hide damage, and a quick sort also turns up the spare carabiner you thought you lost.

faq.q: Does the Teufelberger Kitbag hold a full climbing rope?
faq.a: It is designed to carry a climbing rope and kit. Very long or thick lines may need a larger dedicated rope bag.

faq.q: How do I clean it?
faq.a: Brush off dirt, wipe with mild soap and water, and let it dry open. Avoid solvents.

name: Weaver Small Rope Bag
title: Weaver Small Rope Bag for Climbing Line and Lanyards
meta: The Weaver small rope bag holds a short climbing line, lanyard, or access line and keeps it clean. What fits, how crews use it, and how to pack and store rope.
tagline: A compact Weaver rope bag for shorter lines, lanyards, and access ropes.
summary: The Weaver small rope bag is a compact drawstring-style bag for a shorter climbing line, a rope lanyard, or an access line. It keeps the rope clean, stops tangles in the truck, and makes it easy to grab the right line.
highlights: Easy to tell lines apart in the truck
Good for lanyards and access lines

body.h: Where a small rope bag earns its spot
p: Not every rope needs a big bag. A short climbing line for small trees, a rope lanyard, a spare access line, or a pull rope all fit better in something compact. A small rope bag stops those lines from turning into a knot in the truck box and keeps them clean between jobs.

Using separate bags also helps crews keep track of which rope is which. Label the bag or match it to the rope color so nobody grabs a rigging line when they need the climbing line. See more sizes in our rope bags.
Small bags are also handy for the extra lines on a removal: a tag line, a pull rope for directional felling, or a spare lowering line. Each one comes out ready to use instead of as a tangle.
Feed the rope in hand over hand rather than coiling it, so it pays out without twists. Dry the rope before closing the bag for storage, and keep it away from fuel, bar oil, and battery acid.
Inspect any life-support rope before every climb regardless of how it was stored, and retire it when the maker's guidance says it is done.

faq.q: Will a full-length climbing rope fit in the Weaver small rope bag?
faq.a: It is sized for shorter lines. A full-length climbing rope usually needs a medium or large bag.

faq.q: Can I use it for throw line?
faq.a: You can, but a dedicated throw line bag or cube is easier to throw from without tangles.

name: DMM 6L Tool Bag
title: DMM 6L Tool Bag for Arborist Saddles
meta: The DMM 6L tool bag hangs from your saddle to carry small kit aloft: spare hitch cord, a file, snacks, or a first aid pouch. How to use it and what to pack.
tagline: A 6-liter DMM bag that clips to your saddle to carry small kit in the tree.
summary: The DMM 6L tool bag is a small pouch that hangs from your saddle so small items ride with you in the tree. It is handy for spare hitch cord, a phone, a small first aid kit, or a water bottle on a long climb.
highlights: Keeps small kit within reach aloft

p: Gear loops are for hardware. Everything else, such as a spare split tail, a roll of flagging tape, a file, a snack, or a phone, needs somewhere to live that will not snag on branches or fall out mid-climb. A small saddle bag like the DMM 6-liter tool bag keeps those items closed in and within reach.
Hang it where it will not interfere with your bridge, lanyard, or saw. Most climbers put it toward the back of the saddle. Browse other options in our gear storage section.

body.h: What to carry and what not to
p: Keep it light. A small bag is for small things, and heavy items swinging from your saddle pull on your hips and get in the way when you reposition. A compact first aid kit and a spare hitch cord are good choices for every climb.

Do not hang life-support connections from the bag or its attachment point. Clip it only to a gear loop or accessory point, and follow your saddle maker's instructions about what each attachment is rated for.
Zip or close the bag before you move around the tree. An open pouch dumps its contents the first time you lean back or swing, and anything that falls from the canopy is a hazard to the ground crew.

faq.q: How do I attach the DMM tool bag to my saddle?
faq.a: Clip it to a gear loop or accessory point. Never use a life-support attachment point for storage.

faq.q: Is 6 liters big enough?
faq.a: It holds small items like hitch cord, a phone, tape, and a compact first aid kit. Larger items belong on the ground or on a separate line.

title: Weaver Ditty Bag with First Aid Pouch for Climbers
h1: Weaver Ditty Bag with First Aid Pouch
meta: The Weaver ditty bag with first aid pouch rides on your saddle so small tools and basic first aid supplies go up the tree with you. What to pack and how to use it.
tagline: A saddle ditty bag with a dedicated first aid pouch for climbers.
summary: The Weaver ditty bag with first aid pouch hangs on your saddle and carries small kit in one pocket and first aid supplies in another. It keeps the items you need most in an emergency right on your harness.
highlights: Separate pouch for first aid supplies
Main pocket for small tools and spares
Keeps first aid with the climber aloft
specs: Main bag plus first aid pouch

body.h: First aid that goes up with you
p: A first aid kit in the truck does not help much when a climber cuts a hand 60 feet up. Carrying a small kit on the saddle means a pressure bandage and gloves are available right away. The Weaver ditty bag gives those supplies their own pouch, so they do not get buried under files, tape, and spare cord.
The main bag holds the small things every climber picks up: a spare hitch cord, a file, a marker, a snack. Compare other saddle bags in our gear storage section.

Keeping first aid on every climber's saddle is also a good habit for aerial rescue planning. If a climber is hurt aloft, the rescuer reaches supplies on the casualty's own saddle without a second trip.

Most climbers carry a pressure dressing, gauze, nitrile gloves, and tape at minimum. Check your company's first aid policy and the requirements that apply to your crew. A tourniquet is worth considering for saw work, but only with training on how and when to use it.
Check the kit regularly and replace anything used or expired. Hang the bag from a gear loop, not a life-support attachment point, and keep it clear of your bridge and lanyard.

faq.q: Does the Weaver ditty bag come with first aid supplies?
faq.a: Plan to stock it yourself to match your crew's first aid policy unless the listing says supplies are included.

faq.q: Where should I hang it on my saddle?
faq.a: On a gear loop toward the side or back, where it will not interfere with your bridge, lanyard, or saw.

name: Weaver Ditty Bag
title: Weaver Ditty Bag for Arborist Saddle Storage
meta: The Weaver ditty bag clips to your saddle and holds small kit in the tree: spare hitch cord, files, tape, and snacks. How climbers use it and what to keep in it.
tagline: A small saddle bag for the bits and pieces a climber needs aloft.
summary: The Weaver ditty bag is a small pouch that hangs from your saddle so spare hitch cord, a file, tape, and other small items stay with you in the tree. It keeps loose items off your gear loops and out of the drop zone.
highlights: Low price for an everyday accessory
specs: Small item storage on the saddle

body.h: A home for the small stuff
p: Every climber carries a few things that do not belong on a carabiner: a spare split tail, a chainsaw file, flagging tape, a marker, a granola bar. Stuffed into pockets they fall out; clipped loose they snag. A ditty bag on the saddle keeps them closed in and easy to find.
It also cuts down on dropped items. Anything that falls from the canopy is a hazard to the ground crew. See other saddle bags and storage in our gear storage section.
Ditty bags are cheap enough that many climbers run two: one for spares such as hitch cord and a small pulley, and one for personal items. That keeps the spares clean and easy to find in a hurry.

Hang the ditty bag from a gear loop, not a life-support attachment point, and keep it clear of your bridge, lanyard, and saw. Keep the load light; heavy items swinging on the saddle are tiring and get in the way.
Consider keeping a small first aid kit in it if your saddle does not already carry one. Empty and dry it out now and then so sap, sawdust, and moisture do not build up.

faq.q: What is a ditty bag for arborists?
faq.a: A small pouch that hangs from the saddle to carry small items like spare cord, files, and tape while you climb.

faq.q: Can I clip the ditty bag to my bridge?
faq.a: No. Keep it on a gear loop so nothing interferes with your life-support connections.

name: Edelrid Spring Bag
title: Edelrid Spring Bag for Throw Line Storage
meta: The Edelrid Spring Bag opens wide and folds flat, so throw line flakes out cleanly without tangles. How arborists use it for setting lines and how to pack it.
tagline: A collapsible Edelrid bag that springs open for tangle-free throw line.
summary: The Edelrid Spring Bag is a collapsible throw line bag that pops open when you set it down, so the line can flake in and out cleanly. Fold it flat for storage and spring it open at the tree.
highlights: Throw line pays out without tangles

body.h: Why throw line needs its own storage
p: The Edelrid Spring Bag uses a sprung frame so the bag stands open on its own. That matters when you are stuffing line back in between throws: both hands stay on the line, and the bag does not collapse on you. When the job is done, fold it down and it takes up little room in the truck or gear bag.

Thin throw line tangles faster than anything else in the truck. A loose pile turns into a bird's nest the moment you try to throw from it, and untangling it eats time at the start of every job. Keeping the line in a container that opens wide and lets it flake out cleanly is the easiest fix. Compare options in our gear storage section.

body.h: Throwing from it and caring for it
p: Feed the line in loosely rather than wrapping it, and keep the end tied off inside so it cannot be pulled away. Set the bag on the ground a step back from where you throw so the line peels off the top without catching your feet or brush.

Keep throw line dry and out of the sun between jobs, and away from fuel and bar oil. Before setting a climbing line, check the throw line and weight for cuts or damage, and keep the area under the throw clear of people.

faq.q: How do I fold the Edelrid Spring Bag?
faq.a: Twist and fold the sprung frame down as the instructions show. It takes a little practice the first few times.

faq.q: Will it hold two throw lines?
faq.a: It depends on line length and diameter. Many climbers keep one line per bag to avoid tangles.

p: A medium throw line bag is the everyday size: big enough to stuff a full throw line quickly between attempts without fussing, small enough to toss in a gear bag. The open top lets you feed line in by the handful while you watch the canopy, then throw again straight from the bag.

Thin throw line tangles faster than anything else in the truck. A loose pile turns into a bird's nest the moment you try to throw from it, and untangling it eats time at the start of every job. Keeping the line in a container that opens wide and lets it flake out cleanly is the easiest fix. Compare options in our gear storage section.

body.h: Throwing from it and caring for it
p: Feed the line in loosely rather than wrapping it, and keep the end tied off inside so it cannot be pulled away. Set the bag on the ground a step back from where you throw so the line peels off the top without catching your feet or brush.

Many climbers carry their throw weight in the bag tied to the line, so the whole kit comes out in one grab. Keep the weight on top so it is ready to throw.

faq.q: What size throw line bag do I need?
faq.a: A medium bag suits most single throw lines. Choose larger if you carry a long line or two lines together.

faq.q: Can I store the throw weight in the bag?

title: Weaver Nesting Throwline Storage Bag for Two Lines
meta: The Weaver nesting throwline storage bag lets bags sit inside one another, so you carry more than one throw line in a compact kit. How it works and when to use it.

summary: The Weaver nesting throwline storage bag is designed so bags fit inside one another, letting you carry a spare throw line or a second color without adding bulk. Each line stays in its own bag, so they do not tangle together.
highlights: Bags nest together to save space
Handy for spare or second line
specs: Storing more than one throw line

body.h: Why throw line needs its own storage
p: Climbers who set lines often end up carrying two throw lines: one in use and one spare for when the first hangs up, or a second line for setting a redirect or isolating a limb. Nesting bags let you keep both lines separate without carrying two full-size bags. Pull out the one you need and the other stays packed.

Thin throw line tangles faster than anything else in the truck. A loose pile turns into a bird's nest the moment you try to throw from it, and untangling it eats time at the start of every job. Keeping the line in a container that opens wide and lets it flake out cleanly is the easiest fix. Compare options in our gear storage section.

body.h: Throwing from it and caring for it
p: Feed the line in loosely rather than wrapping it, and keep the end tied off inside so it cannot be pulled away. Set the bag on the ground a step back from where you throw so the line peels off the top without catching your feet or brush.

Keep throw line dry and out of the sun between jobs, and away from fuel and bar oil. Before setting a climbing line, check the throw line and weight for cuts or damage, and keep the area under the throw clear of people.
Using two different line colors helps when both lines are in the tree at once, since you can tell at a glance which one to pull.

faq.q: Why carry two throw lines?
faq.a: A spare saves time when the first line hangs up, and a second line helps when isolating a crotch or setting a redirect.

faq.q: Do the nested bags tangle the lines?
faq.a: No. Each line stays in its own bag, which is the point of the design.

name: Weaver Small Throwline Storage Bag
title: Weaver Small Throwline Storage Bag for Arborists
meta: The Weaver small throwline storage bag keeps a throw line flaked and tangle-free in a compact size that rides in any gear bag. How to pack it and throw from it.
tagline: A compact Weaver bag for a single throw line.
summary: The Weaver small throwline storage bag is a compact bag for one throw line. It keeps the line flaked and clean, and it is small enough to clip to a gear bag or tuck into a pocket of your kit.
highlights: Compact size for one throw line
Easy to carry in any kit

body.h: Why throw line needs its own storage
p: A small throw line bag suits climbers who carry a shorter line, or who want a light bag that fits in a saddle bag or climbing kit. It is just big enough for the line and weight, so it does not take up room you need for other gear.

Thin throw line tangles faster than anything else in the truck. A loose pile turns into a bird's nest the moment you try to throw from it, and untangling it eats time at the start of every job. Keeping the line in a container that opens wide and lets it flake out cleanly is the easiest fix. Compare options in our gear storage section.

body.h: Throwing from it and caring for it
p: Feed the line in loosely rather than wrapping it, and keep the end tied off inside so it cannot be pulled away. Set the bag on the ground a step back from where you throw so the line peels off the top without catching your feet or brush.

Keep throw line dry and out of the sun between jobs, and away from fuel and bar oil. Before setting a climbing line, check the throw line and weight for cuts or damage, and keep the area under the throw clear of people.
A small bag is also a good choice for a backup line that rides in your saddle kit, ready for the day the main line gets stuck high in the canopy.

faq.q: Is the small bag big enough for a full throw line?
faq.a: It suits a single, shorter throw line. If you carry a long line, a medium bag is easier to stuff quickly.

faq.q: Small bag or throw line cube?
faq.a: A cube holds its shape and stands open; a small bag is lighter and packs down. Both work.

name: Weaver Throw Line Cube
title: Weaver Throw Line Cube for Tangle-Free Throw Line
meta: The Weaver throw line cube stands open on the ground so your throw line feeds in fast and pays out clean. How climbers use a throw cube and how to pack it.
tagline: A Weaver throw line cube that stands open for fast, tangle-free line setting.
summary: The Weaver throw line cube is a square throw line container that holds its shape on the ground, so you can stuff line in quickly and throw again without tangles. It is one of the most common ways climbers keep throw line under control.
highlights: Holds its shape and stands open

body.h: Why throw line needs its own storage
p: A throw cube sits on the ground like an open box. Between throws you feed the line straight in by the handful, and when you throw again it lifts off the top without snagging. That simple shape is why the cube is a favorite for climbers who set a lot of lines in a day.

Thin throw line tangles faster than anything else in the truck. A loose pile turns into a bird's nest the moment you try to throw from it, and untangling it eats time at the start of every job. Keeping the line in a container that opens wide and lets it flake out cleanly is the easiest fix. Compare options in our gear storage section.

body.h: Throwing from it and caring for it
p: Feed the line in loosely rather than wrapping it, and keep the end tied off inside so it cannot be pulled away. Set the bag on the ground a step back from where you throw so the line peels off the top without catching your feet or brush.

Keep throw line dry and out of the sun between jobs, and away from fuel and bar oil. Before setting a climbing line, check the throw line and weight for cuts or damage, and keep the area under the throw clear of people.
If the cube gets packed with sawdust or leaves, turn it out and shake it clean. Debris in the bag ends up wrapped in the line and makes every throw less predictable.

faq.q: Does the Weaver throw line cube fold down?
faq.a: Throw cubes are designed to collapse for transport and open up at the tree.

faq.q: Can I keep two lines in one cube?
faq.a: It is better to use one line per cube so they cannot tangle together.

name: Armor Prus 10mm Eye-to-Eye Prusik
title: Armor Prus 10mm Eye-to-Eye Prusik Hitch Cord
meta: The Armor Prus 10mm eye-to-eye prusik is a hitch cord with an eye at each end for doubled-rope climbing. Rope compatibility, hitch choice, and inspection tips.
tagline: A 10mm eye-to-eye hitch cord for tending a friction hitch on doubled-rope systems.
summary: The Armor Prus 10mm eye-to-eye prusik is a hitch cord with an eye at each end, used to tie a friction hitch such as a Distel or VT on your climbing line. It is a core piece of a doubled-rope climbing system and a wear item every climber replaces regularly.
highlights: Eye at each end for clean connections
For friction hitches such as Distel or VT

p: A friction hitch only works when the hitch cord and climbing line suit each other. The cord should usually be a bit smaller than or close to the rope's diameter, and the cover materials need to grip without melting or glazing. A 10mm hitch cord pairs with a range of common arborist climbing lines, but the right hitch, wraps, and braids depend on your rope.
Set it up low and test it on the ground. If it slips, add a wrap or change the hitch; if it binds, back off. Compare lengths and other cords in our eye and eye prusiks.

Eye-to-eye cords connect to your bridge or climbing system with a carabiner through both eyes, so they are quick to swap when worn. Length matters too: too long and the hitch tends poorly, too short and the hitch will not dress properly.

Hitch cord takes the most heat and abrasion of anything in your system. Check it before each climb for glazing, stiff spots, cover damage, and wear at the eyes. Pull it from service if it has been shock loaded, contaminated with chemicals, or if you find any damage.
Use it within the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained on friction hitches before you rely on one. Many climbers carry a spare in their saddle bag.

faq.q: What climbing rope works with a 10mm eye-to-eye prusik?
faq.a: Many common arborist climbing lines in the 11 to 13mm range work, but always test the hitch on your own rope and follow the maker's guidance.

faq.q: How often should I replace hitch cord?
faq.a: When inspection shows glazing, cover damage, stiffness, or wear at the eyes. Busy climbers replace it often.

name: Teufelberger 8mm Ocean Polyester Thimble Loop
title: Teufelberger 8mm Ocean Polyester Thimble Loop
meta: The Teufelberger Ocean Polyester thimble loop is an 8mm polyester loop with a thimble eye for prusik and attachment work. How climbers use it and how to inspect it.
tagline: An 8mm polyester loop with a thimble eye for prusik and hitch setups.
summary: The Teufelberger Ocean Polyester thimble loop is an 8mm polyester prusik loop with a thimble that protects the eye where it meets hardware. Climbers and riggers use loops like this for friction hitches, short tethers, and attachment points.
highlights: Thimble protects the eye from wear
Useful for prusiks and short attachments

p: A thimble keeps the eye of a loop open and gives a carabiner a smooth, hard surface to bear on. That cuts wear at the point where soft cord meets metal, especially on a loop that gets clipped and unclipped all day. An 8mm polyester loop is a handy size for prusiks on rigging lines, a short attachment for a pulley, or a backup hitch.
Polyester stretches little and stands up to abrasion, which suits these jobs. Compare other cords and loops in our hitch cord and split tails.

Rigging crews use short loops like this to attach a pulley or block to a sling, or to tie a prusik onto a lowering line for a mechanical advantage setup. Having a few spares in the rigging bag saves time on the job.

An 8mm loop is not a substitute for a climbing hitch cord unless the maker approves it for that use with your rope. Check the rated strength, test any hitch on the ground first, and never exceed what the loop is rated for.

Inspect the cord, the thimble, and the splice or stitching before each use. Retire it after a shock load or if you find cuts, glazing, or a deformed thimble. Follow the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice.

faq.q: Can I use an 8mm thimble loop as my climbing friction hitch?
faq.a: Only if the maker approves it for that use with your rope. Most climbers use a dedicated hitch cord closer to their rope diameter.

faq.q: What does the thimble do?
faq.a: It keeps the eye open and protects the cord from wear where it contacts a carabiner or pulley.

name: Rock Exotica Enforcer with Case
title: Rock Exotica Enforcer Load Cell with Case
meta: The Rock Exotica Enforcer is a load cell that measures forces in rope systems. How tree crews use it to check rigging loads and train climbers, and what to know.
tagline: A portable load cell for measuring real forces in rigging and climbing systems.
summary: The Rock Exotica Enforcer is a portable load cell that clips inline in a rope system and records the forces it sees. Arborists use it to measure rigging loads, compare techniques, and teach crews what a drop actually puts on the gear.
highlights: Measures force inline in a rope system
Useful for rigging training and testing

p: Most rigging decisions are made by feel: how big a piece, how much run, how hard to let it run. A load cell replaces guesswork with a number. Put the Enforcer inline between the rigging point and the block or lowering device, take a cut, and you see the peak force the system saw. Do the same piece with more friction or a shorter drop and the difference is obvious.
That makes it a strong training tool. New climbers learn quickly why a small piece dropped a few feet loads a rigging point more than they expected. See more specialty gear in our other gear section.

A load cell is an instrument, not a rigging connector to leave in the system. Use it within its rated range and the maker's instructions, check the batteries and calibration as directed, and keep it in the case between jobs.

Testing rigging loads means setting up controlled drops, so plan them carefully. Keep everyone out of the drop zone, use rated hardware throughout, and follow ANSI Z133 practice. Treat the numbers as a guide to better rigging, not permission to push gear closer to its limits.
Record what you test. A short log of piece size, drop, friction setup, and peak load gives your crew a reference that is far more useful than memory.

faq.q: What is the Rock Exotica Enforcer used for in tree work?
faq.a: Measuring rigging and climbing loads for training, testing techniques, and understanding how hard a drop loads the gear.

faq.q: Can I leave it rigged in the system all day?
faq.a: It is meant for measurement and training. Follow Rock Exotica's instructions on how it may be used and loaded.

name: Teufelberger Rope Tarp
title: Teufelberger Rope Tarp for Clean Climbing Rope
meta: The Teufelberger rope tarp gives your climbing line a clean place to lie at the base of the tree. Why a rope tarp extends rope life and how climbers use it.
tagline: A ground tarp that keeps your climbing rope out of the dirt at the base of the tree.
summary: The Teufelberger rope tarp is a ground sheet for your climbing line, laid at the base of the tree so the rope stays out of the dirt, sawdust, and mud while you climb. Many styles also wrap up to carry the rope.
highlights: Cuts grit damage to the braid
Easy to spot the rope pile
Folds up with the rope inside
Quick to lay out and pack

body.h: Why lay rope on a tarp
p: Grit that gets into a climbing rope stays there, grinding the fibers each time the line runs through your hitch, pulley, or friction saver. A tarp at the base of the tree keeps the tail of the rope out of the dirt, sawdust, and wet grass for the whole climb. It also marks where the rope is, which helps the ground crew keep wood and the chipper away from it.
At the end of the day the rope gets flaked back onto the tarp and wrapped up for the ride home. Browse other specialty items in our other gear section.
Tarps are also handy on hard surfaces. Driveways and patios are rough on rope, and the tarp gives the line a smooth surface instead of concrete.
Shake the tarp out before folding so sawdust and leaves do not end up inside the bundle. Dry it and the rope before storing, and keep both away from fuel, bar oil, and battery acid.
A tarp protects the rope from dirt but does not replace inspection. Run the rope through your hands before every climb and retire it according to Teufelberger's guidance and ANSI Z133 practice.

faq.q: Is a rope tarp better than a rope bag?
faq.a: Both keep rope clean. A tarp gives a flat, visible spot at the tree; a bag is faster to carry and deploy. Many climbers use both.

faq.q: Can I use a rope tarp for rigging lines?
faq.a: Yes, though rigging lines are often long and heavy, so a large tarp or bag works best.

name: SMC Radius Rings
title: SMC Radius Rings for Climbing and Friction Savers
meta: SMC Radius rings are smooth, rounded rings for building friction savers, adjustable bridges, and anchor setups. Where climbers use them and how to inspect them.
tagline: Smooth, rounded rings for friction savers, bridges, and anchor builds.
summary: SMC Radius rings are rounded metal rings used to build friction savers, adjustable bridges, and anchors in tree climbing systems. A ring gives rope a smooth surface to run over and a simple connection with no moving parts.
highlights: Smooth radius for rope to run over
Useful for friction savers and bridges
From a long-time rescue hardware maker

body.h: Where rings fit in a climbing kit
p: Rings show up all over a modern climbing system. A pair on a length of rope makes a ring friction saver. A ring on a rope bridge lets your climbing system slide side to side as you work. A ring at an anchor gives you a smooth redirect without a carabiner gate in the way. Because there is no gate to open and nothing to rotate, rings are simple and easy to check.
Pick the size and strength that suit the job and the other hardware they meet. See all sizes in our rings section.

Ring size changes how rope behaves. A larger radius is gentler on the line and lets friction hitches and hardware pass more easily, while a smaller ring is lighter. Match ring size to the rope and the other hardware in the system.
Check rings before each use for grooves worn by rope, burrs, cracks, and deformation. A groove that catches your fingernail is a reason to retire the ring, because a sharp edge will cut rope fast.

Use rings only for the loads and configurations the maker rates them for, and keep them from being side-loaded against a stem. Life-support use must follow the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice.

faq.q: What are SMC Radius rings used for in tree climbing?
faq.a: Building ring friction savers, as the sliding point on a rope bridge, and for anchors or redirects.

faq.q: When should I retire a climbing ring?
faq.a: When you find grooves, burrs, cracks, or deformation, or after a serious shock load.

name: DMM Nexus Swivel
title: DMM Nexus Swivel for Climbing and Rigging
meta: The DMM Nexus swivel lets connected gear spin freely so ropes and lanyards do not twist. How arborists use it in climbing and rigging setups, and what to inspect.
tagline: A DMM swivel with multiple attachment points to stop twists in your system.
summary: The DMM Nexus swivel is a bearing swivel that lets the parts of a climbing or rigging system rotate freely, so ropes and lanyards do not twist up. Its larger attachment eye can take more than one connector, which makes it useful as a small hub.

p: Every time a climber spins on a single line or a rigged piece rotates on the way down, twist goes into the rope. Over a day it builds up into kinks and hockles that make devices and hitches run badly. A swivel between the rope and your saddle, or between the rigging line and the load, lets that rotation happen at the bearing instead.
The Nexus adds a larger attachment eye, so you can clip a second connector for a positioning lanyard, a pulley, or a tool line. Compare other models in our swivels.

In rigging, a swivel between the lowering line and a heavy piece lets the wood rotate as it comes down without spinning the rope into kinks. That keeps the line running clean through the block and the lowering device.

Check that the swivel spins smoothly before each use, with no grinding, play, or flat spots. Look for cracks, sharp edges, and wear where connectors bear on the eyes. Retire it after a shock load or any sign of damage.

Load it only in the directions and configurations DMM approves, and make sure every connector on it is oriented correctly and closed. Life-support use must follow the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice.

faq.q: Where should a swivel go in a climbing system?
faq.a: Common spots are between the bridge and the climbing device, or at the end of a rope in an SRS setup. Follow the maker's instructions for your system.

faq.q: Can I use the DMM Nexus swivel for rigging?
faq.a: Swivels are used in rigging to stop line twist. Check DMM's rated strength against your expected loads.

name: Petzl Swivel Open
title: Petzl Swivel Open: Openable Swivel for Climbers
meta: The Petzl Swivel Open is a swivel with an openable side, so it goes straight onto a saddle bridge or fixed loop. How climbers use it and what to check before each climb.
tagline: An openable Petzl swivel that installs directly on a bridge or fixed loop.
summary: The Petzl Swivel Open is a bearing swivel with one side that opens, so you can put it on a saddle bridge or closed loop without taking anything apart. It stops your climbing system from twisting while you work and spin in the tree.
highlights: Fits on bridges and fixed loops

p: Most swivels have two closed eyes, so you need connectors on both sides. The Swivel Open lets you open one side and put it straight onto a rope bridge or another closed loop. That removes a carabiner from the stack, shortens the system, and keeps the swivel's orientation consistent.
Climbers often use it on the bridge with the climbing device below it, so the device can rotate as you move around the tree without twisting the rope. See other options in our swivels.

In single-rope setups, the swivel also keeps the device oriented to the rope as you work out a limb and come back, so the line does not twist up between the anchor and your saddle. Less twist means a smoother descent and fewer kinks at the end of the day.

Before each climb, check that the swivel turns freely, the openable side closes and locks fully, and there are no cracks, sharp edges, or worn spots. Retire it after a shock load or any sign of damage.

Make sure the opening side is closed and secured every time you load it. Use it only in the configurations Petzl approves, and follow the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice for life-support gear.

faq.q: Why use the Petzl Swivel Open instead of a regular swivel?
faq.a: It opens on one side, so you can install it directly on a bridge or loop without an extra carabiner.

faq.q: Is the Petzl Swivel Open life-support rated?
faq.a: It is built for work-at-height systems. Check the markings and Petzl's instructions for its rated strength and approved uses.

name: Husqvarna Functional Helmet with Wheel Ratchet Adjustment
title: Husqvarna Functional Helmet with Wheel Ratchet
h1: Husqvarna Functional Helmet with Wheel Ratchet Adjustment
meta: The Husqvarna Functional helmet pairs a hard hat, mesh visor, and ear muffs with a wheel ratchet. Who it suits on a tree crew and how it differs from a climbing helmet.
tagline: A forestry helmet system with visor, ear muffs, and quick wheel ratchet fit.
summary: The Husqvarna Functional helmet is a forestry helmet system with a hard shell, mesh face visor, and ear muffs, fitted with a wheel ratchet for quick sizing. It suits saw work on the ground: felling, bucking, and limbing.
highlights: Hard hat, visor, and ear muffs in one
Mesh visor keeps chips off your face

p: Running a saw on the ground means three hazards at once: falling wood, flying chips, and noise. A forestry helmet system like the Husqvarna Functional handles all three with one piece of kit. The visor flips down for cutting and up for talking, and the ear muffs swing out of the way when the saw is off.
The wheel ratchet lets you tighten or loosen the fit with gloves on, which helps when switching between a beanie in winter and a bare head in summer. Compare other helmets in our helmets section.
It is a good fit for ground workers on a tree crew and for homeowners who run a saw occasionally. Everything is in one package, so there is no guessing about which visor or ear muffs fit the shell.

This is a forestry helmet, not a climbing helmet. Climbing helmets have a chin strap system designed to keep the helmet on in a fall and are tested for different impacts. If you climb or work from a lift, use a helmet rated for that work, as ANSI Z133 and your employer require.

Check the helmet's markings for the standards it meets, and replace the shell after a heavy impact or at the age the maker recommends. A mesh visor protects from chips but is not safety eyewear, so wear rated glasses too.

faq.q: Can I climb in the Husqvarna Functional helmet?
faq.a: It is designed for ground forestry work. Climbers should use a helmet made and rated for climbing, with a proper chin strap.

faq.q: Do I still need safety glasses with the mesh visor?
faq.a: Yes. A mesh visor stops chips but not fine dust or small fragments, so wear rated eye protection underneath.

name: Petzl Vertex Helmet
title: Petzl Vertex Helmet for Arborists and Climbers
meta: The Petzl Vertex helmet is a comfortable work-at-height helmet with a secure chin strap and accessory slots. Why arborists wear it, fit tips, and add-on options.
tagline: A comfortable work-at-height helmet that climbers wear all day.
summary: The Petzl Vertex helmet is a work-at-height helmet built for climbing and rope access, with a six-point textile suspension, an adjustable chin strap, and slots for a visor, ear muffs, and headlamp. It is one of the most common climbing helmets on tree crews.
highlights: Slots for visor, ear muffs, and headlamp

p: A climbing helmet gets worn all day, so comfort decides whether it stays on your head. The Vertex sits low and stable, with a suspension that spreads the weight and a chin strap that keeps it on when you lean, swing, or look up into the canopy. Fit adjusts quickly, which helps when you add or take off a beanie as the day warms up.
Accessory slots let you build it into a full setup: a mesh or clear visor, ear muffs, and a headlamp for early starts or storm work. See other models in our helmets section.
Bright colors help the ground crew track the climber in the canopy, which matters when wood is coming down and everyone needs to know where the climber is.

Adjust the headband so the helmet sits level and does not rock, then snug the chin strap. Check the label for the standards your version meets, and make sure it fits what ANSI Z133 and your employer require for climbing and aerial work.

Inspect the shell, suspension, and strap before each use. Replace the helmet after a significant impact even if you see no damage, and follow Petzl's guidance on service life. Keep it out of the sun on the dash and away from solvents.

faq.q: Is the Petzl Vertex helmet good for tree climbing?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the most widely used helmets among climbing arborists. Check that your version meets the standards your work requires.

faq.q: Can I add ear muffs and a visor?
faq.a: Yes. The Vertex has slots for compatible visors, ear muffs, and headlamps.

name: Petzl Vertex Vent Hi-Viz Climbing Helmet
title: Petzl Vertex Vent Hi-Viz Climbing Helmet
h1: Petzl Vertex Vent Hi-Viz Climbing Helmet
meta: The Petzl Vertex Vent hi-viz helmet adds closable vents and a high-visibility shell to the Vertex design. Why roadside and storm crews like it, plus fit tips.
tagline: A vented, high-visibility Vertex helmet for climbers who need to be seen.
summary: The Petzl Vertex Vent Hi-Viz is the vented version of the Vertex climbing helmet in a high-visibility shell, with reflective bands for low light. It suits climbers and bucket operators who work near roads or in poor light and want airflow on hot days.
highlights: Chin strap built for work at height
Slots for visor, ear muffs, and headlamp

p: Roadside work, utility clearance, and storm cleanup put crews close to traffic and often in bad light. A hi-viz helmet with reflective bands makes the climber or bucket operator easier to spot. The vents help on hot days, and they can be closed when you need protection from rain, sawdust, or debris.
It takes the same accessories as other Vertex models: visors, ear muffs, and headlamps. Compare models in our helmets section.

The chin strap and fit system match the standard Vertex, so climbers who already know that helmet get the same feel with more airflow and visibility. That makes it an easy upgrade for crews that do a lot of roadside work or need to be seen.

Adjust the headband so the helmet sits level, then snug the chin strap. Vented helmets and closed-shell helmets can carry different certifications, so check your version's label and confirm it meets what ANSI Z133 and your employer require, especially for electrical hazard work near lines.

Inspect the shell, suspension, vents, and strap before each use. Replace the helmet after a significant impact and follow Petzl's guidance on service life. A dirty hi-viz shell loses much of its visibility, so keep it clean.

faq.q: Can I wear a vented helmet near power lines?
faq.a: Vented helmets are generally not rated for electrical protection. Near energized lines, use a helmet rated for that hazard and follow ANSI Z133 and your employer's rules.

faq.q: Does a hi-viz helmet replace a hi-viz vest?
faq.a: No. It adds visibility, but roadside work usually still requires high-visibility apparel.

name: Buckingham Ergo Pro Y-Style Retro-Fit Fall Arrest Harness
title: Buckingham Ergo Pro Y-Style Fall Arrest Harness
h1: Buckingham Ergo Pro Y-Style Retro-Fit Fall Arrest Harness
meta: The Buckingham Ergo Pro Y-style harness retro-fits an upper body harness to an Ergo saddle for aerial lift and fall arrest work. Fit, use, and what to check.
tagline: A Y-style upper body harness that retro-fits a Buckingham Ergo saddle for fall arrest.
summary: The Buckingham Ergo Pro Y-style fall arrest harness is an upper body add-on that turns a compatible Ergo saddle into a setup with a dorsal attachment for fall arrest. It suits climbers who also work from aerial lifts and want one harness for both jobs.
highlights: One harness for climbing and lift work
From an established US saddle maker

body.h: Why add fall arrest to a saddle
p: A tree saddle is built for work positioning, not for catching a free fall. When you work from an aerial lift, the rules usually call for a full body harness with a dorsal attachment and a lanyard to the boom or bucket anchor. A retro-fit harness lets crews who switch between climbing and lift work use one compatible setup instead of swapping between two harnesses.
The Y-style straps sit over the shoulders and meet at the back, where the fall arrest attachment rides. Browse other parts and harnesses in our saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.
It also suits crews where climbers rotate into the bucket for part of the day. Going from climbing to the lift without changing harnesses saves time and keeps a familiar saddle on every climber.

Only fit this harness to the Buckingham saddle models it is designed for, and assemble it exactly as the instructions describe. A combined harness is only certified as a system when the parts are approved to work together. Check the labels and instructions for the standards it meets before using it for fall arrest.

Inspect webbing, stitching, buckles, and the dorsal D-ring before each use. Retire any part that has arrested a fall. Get trained on aerial lift fall protection and follow ANSI Z133, ANSI A92, and your employer's rules.

faq.q: Will the Buckingham Ergo Pro fall arrest harness fit my saddle?
faq.a: It is made for specific Buckingham Ergo saddle models. Check compatibility before buying.

faq.q: Can I use a regular tree saddle for aerial lift fall arrest?
faq.a: A saddle alone is not a fall arrest harness. Use a full body harness or an approved combined system.

name: Petzl Sequoia Adjustable Bridge
title: Petzl Sequoia Adjustable Bridge Replacement
meta: The Petzl Sequoia adjustable bridge replaces a worn bridge on Sequoia saddles, so you can keep the harness in service. Fit, setup, and inspection tips for climbers.
tagline: A replacement adjustable bridge for Petzl Sequoia saddles.
summary: The Petzl Sequoia adjustable bridge is the replacement bridge for Sequoia tree climbing saddles. The bridge is the most worn part of the saddle, so replacing it on schedule keeps the harness in service.
highlights: Swap a worn bridge without a new saddle

p: Every climb runs a carabiner or swivel back and forth across the bridge. It slides as you move around the tree and takes the weight each time you sit back. Over a season that wear adds up faster than on any other part of the saddle. Replacing the bridge when it is worn keeps the saddle working without buying a whole new harness.

Adjustable length lets you set where the attachment point sits relative to your body, which affects comfort and how the climbing system hangs. Browse more saddle parts in our saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.
Many climbers keep a spare bridge in their kit. A bridge can be cut or damaged on the job, and having a factory replacement on hand means the saddle is back in service the same day.

Install the bridge exactly as Petzl describes for your Sequoia model, and check that every connection is correct before you load it. If you are unsure, have a qualified person check it before you climb.

Inspect the bridge before every climb for cuts, glazing, flattened spots, and wear where hardware rides. Replace it at the first sign of damage or as Petzl's instructions require. Life-support gear must follow the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice.

faq.q: Will the Petzl Sequoia bridge fit other saddles?
faq.a: It is made for Sequoia saddles. Check Petzl's compatibility information before fitting it to anything else.

faq.q: How often should I replace my bridge?
faq.a: Whenever inspection shows wear or damage. Heavy users often replace bridges more than once a year.

name: Petzl Shoulder Strap for Sequoia
title: Petzl Sequoia Shoulder Strap for Gear Weight Support
meta: The Petzl Sequoia shoulder strap moves gear weight from your hips to your shoulders on a loaded saddle. How it fits, who needs it, and what it is not rated for.
tagline: Shoulder straps that take the weight of a loaded Sequoia saddle off your hips.
summary: The Petzl Sequoia shoulder strap set helps carry the weight of a loaded Sequoia saddle on your shoulders instead of your hips. It keeps the saddle from sagging when it is full of hardware and a saw.
highlights: Spreads gear weight across the shoulders
Keeps a loaded saddle from sagging

p: A fully loaded saddle can carry several pounds of carabiners, lanyards, a handsaw, and a top-handle saw. All of that hangs from your hips, and by mid-afternoon you feel it. Shoulder straps take part of that load and stop the saddle from sliding down when you are on the ground between climbs.
They also help when walking to the tree in your saddle, and some climbers find the waist belt sits better with straps on. Browse more saddle parts in our saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.

Shoulder straps also give you a few more places to carry light items close to the chest, which keeps hardware from crowding the gear loops at your hips. Fit them snug enough to carry weight but loose enough that you can still twist and reach freely in the tree.

These straps carry gear weight. They do not turn a saddle into a full body harness for fall arrest. If you need fall arrest, for example in an aerial lift, use a harness or chest component rated and approved for that use.
Fit them according to Petzl's instructions so they do not interfere with your bridge or attachment points. Check the webbing and buckles regularly, and replace worn parts.

faq.q: Do Sequoia shoulder straps make it a fall arrest harness?
faq.a: No. They support gear weight only. Fall arrest needs a harness rated for it.

faq.q: Will they fit other Petzl saddles?
faq.a: They are made for Sequoia saddles. Check Petzl's compatibility information for other models.

name: Petzl Top Chest Harness
title: Petzl Top Chest Harness for Sit Harnesses
meta: The Petzl Top chest harness pairs with a compatible Petzl sit harness to keep you upright and carry gear. How climbers use it and what to check before use.
tagline: A Petzl chest harness that pairs with a sit harness for support and gear carry.
summary: The Petzl Top chest harness is a chest harness that connects to a compatible Petzl sit harness. It helps keep you upright when hanging, spreads gear weight across the shoulders, and can be used to tend a chest-mounted ascender in rope systems.
highlights: Pairs with compatible Petzl sit harnesses
Helps keep you upright on rope
Can carry a chest ascender setup

p: A sit harness alone lets you hang comfortably, but on long ascents or when working with a lot of gear it can be hard to stay upright. A chest harness like the Petzl Top connects to the sit harness and holds your torso in position. In single-rope systems it can also help set up a chest-mounted ascender or a rope-tending pulley.
It takes some weight off the hips too, which helps on long days with a full gear load. Browse more saddle parts in our saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.
Some climbers add a chest harness only for long single-rope ascents and leave it off for pruning days. It is easy to fit and remove, so you can match your setup to the job.

Use it only with the sit harnesses Petzl lists as compatible, and connect it exactly as the instructions show. A chest harness on its own is not a fall arrest harness, so check how Petzl rates the combined system before using it for fall arrest.

Inspect webbing, stitching, and buckles before each use, and replace any part showing damage. Climbing systems must follow the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and you should be trained on any ascent system you use.

faq.q: Does the Petzl Top work with a Sequoia saddle?
faq.a: Check Petzl's compatibility list for your saddle model before buying.

faq.q: Is a chest harness a fall arrest harness?
faq.a: Not by itself. Check how Petzl rates the combined chest and sit harness system.
